title: India Has Now Served Notices to Every Major Messaging App Over Usernames. The Crackdown Is Widening.
excerpt: After freezing WhatsApp's username rollout, the government is now demanding answers from Telegram and Signal. Indian platform Arattai has already surrendered the feature entirely.
body:
India's crackdown on messaging anonymity is no longer a WhatsApp story. It is now a platform-wide regulatory offensive.

On Thursday, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued formal notices to Telegram and Signal, demanding both platforms explain the safeguards built into their username features — the same anonymity tools that let users message each other without sharing phone numbers.

The notices came barely 24 hours after the government served WhatsApp's parent company Meta with a pointed letter: freeze your planned username rollout in India, justify why the feature should exist at all, or face action under the IT Act. WhatsApp was given three days to respond.

## The Government's Argument

The core concern is impersonation. Officials believe that username-based messaging — where someone can contact you without knowing your phone number — will "materially increase" cases of phishing, digital arrest scams, and financial fraud. In a country where cybercrime complaints are rising steeply and "digital arrest" scams have duped thousands, the ministry views anonymity features as attack surface expansion.

"Government has asked Telegram why the feature should be there," a government source told reporters, framing the question not as a technical query but an existential challenge to the feature itself.

## The Platforms' Positions

The three platforms are in very different positions. Telegram and Signal have had active username features for years. WhatsApp has only announced plans to introduce them — the feature is not yet live.

WhatsApp has pushed back, albeit carefully. The company said it has built "multiple layers of defense against scams" into the feature, including limits on how many new people an account can contact and blocks on repeated attempts to guess a user's username. It also held back high-profile names so they can only be claimed by legitimate owners.

Signal, which is built around privacy as a core proposition, faces a more ideological confrontation. Its username system was specifically designed to let users communicate without revealing their phone numbers — the exact capability India's regulators now question.

## A Pattern of Escalation

The username notices are part of a broader pattern. India temporarily blocked Telegram just weeks ago — partly over the same anonymity concerns — during the NEET-UG re-examination period. The government has spent years sparring with Elon Musk's X over content-takedown orders. And the IT Rules of 2021 already impose strict compliance obligations on "significant social media intermediaries."

The domestic tech ecosystem is already adapting. Arattai, a Zoho-backed messaging platform, announced it would disable its username-based account feature entirely. Founder Sridhar Vembu wrote on X that the decision was made "to comply with the regulatory change."

## The Kunal Shah Irony

The timing carries a bitter irony. Just days before the crackdown, Meta named CRED founder Kunal Shah as WhatsApp's new global head — a rare appointment of an Indian entrepreneur to lead one of the world's biggest tech products, underscoring India's weight as WhatsApp's largest market with more than 500 million users.

Shah's appointment was meant to signal Meta's deep commitment to India. Instead, his first crisis in the role may be navigating a standoff between his new employer and the government of his home country.

## What NRIs Should Know

For the millions of diaspora Indians who rely on WhatsApp, Telegram, and Signal to stay in touch with family, the regulatory direction matters. If India forces platforms to tie usernames to verified phone numbers or to disable the feature entirely, it could limit how diaspora users manage their privacy when communicating across borders. The government's push for accountability is real. So is the risk of overreach.

*Sources: Reuters, Outlook Business, The Hindu BusinessLine, Techlusive, Inshorts*
